ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: Figure A shows an ideal transformer, with the primary coil on the left connected to an AC power supply, and an ammeter A connected in series in the primary-coil circuit; the secondary coil on the right is connected to a light bulb. Figure B shows that the voltage of the power supply connected to the primary coil changes sinusoidally with time, the vertical axis is u/V, the peak value of the waveform is marked as +220√2 V, and the trough value is marked as -220√2 V. Reasoning: The effective value of a sinusoidal alternating current is equal to the peak value divided by √2, so the effective value of the primary-coil voltage is Vp = 220√2 / √2 = 220 V. The problem gives that the turns ratio of the primary and secondary coils is 10:1, and an ideal transformer satisfies Vp/Vs = Np/Ns = 10, therefore the effective value of the secondary-coil voltage is Vs = 220/10 = 22 V. The light bulb consumes power of 60 W, and the input power of an ideal transformer is equal to the output power, so the input power of the primary coil is also 60 W. The ammeter reading is the effective value of the primary-coil current, Ip = Pp/Vp = 60/220 ≈ 0.273 A.

method.method_draft: First inspect the image: Figure A shows an ideal transformer with the source and ammeter on the primary side and a bulb on the secondary side. Figure B shows the primary voltage is sinusoidal, with peak value marked as +220√2 V and -220√2 V, so its RMS/effective value is 220 V. From the text, use the primary-to-secondary turns ratio 10:1, so for an ideal transformer Vp/Vs = Np/Ns = 10; therefore Vs = 220/10 = 22 V. From the text, the bulb consumes 60 W; for an ideal transformer, input power equals output power, so Pp = Ps = 60 W. Then the primary ammeter reads the primary RMS current Ip = Pp/Vp = 60/220 ≈ 0.273 A.
